title: NYC Reduces UBT Credit: What High-Income Taxpayers Should Know
summary: High-income NYC taxpayers may be in for an unwelcome surprise. See what the UBT credit change could mean for you.
body_markdown:
For high-income New York City residents who own an interest in a partnership, LLC, or other unincorporated business, a change to the city’s unincorporated business tax (UBT) credit could mean an unwelcome surprise.


The city reduced its UBT credit for residents with NYC taxable income of $1 million or more, applying the new rules retroactively to tax years beginning on or after Jan. 1, 2026.


## What Changed With the UBT Credit?


Eligible NYC residents can claim a credit against their city personal income tax for a portion of the UBT paid by a partnership in which they hold an interest or a business they operate as a proprietor.


Previously, the credit was generally capped at 23% for residents with NYC taxable income of $142,000 or more. The new structure uses these income brackets:


- **$142,000 to under $1 million:** The credit remains at 23%.
- **$1 million to under $1.25 million:** The credit gradually decreases from 23% to 15%.
- **$1.25 million or more:** The credit is capped at 15%.


## Why the Change Matters for High-Income Taxpayers


For affected high-income pass-through business owners, a smaller UBT credit can mean a higher NYC personal income tax obligation. But the impact may not stop with the final tax bill.


Because the reduction applies retroactively to Jan. 1, 2026, estimated tax payments made earlier in the year under the previous credit structure may no longer reflect the taxpayer’s projected liability. That makes it important to take another look at 2026 estimates rather than assume earlier calculations still hold.


## Key Tax Planning Considerations for 2026


With the UBT credit change applying retroactively, affected taxpayers and businesses should take another look at their 2026 tax planning, including:


- Revisit 2026 tax projections and estimated payments.
- Determine whether catch-up payments or safe harbor calculations should be reconsidered.
- Evaluate the potential impact of the NYC pass-through entity tax (PTET) election for future tax years for partnerships with NYC resident partners.


Keep in mind that there is no NYC Department of Finance guidance as of this publication date on potential penalty relief for estimated tax underpayments attributable to the retroactive reduction.

Connect with a CBIZ advisor to assess how the reduced UBT credit affects your NYC tax position and identify which payment or planning adjustments deserve attention before year-end.
